portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But that's an option open to ACMA—to make a recommendation. If the ABC were to refuse, it is open to ACMA, under section 153, to report the matter to the communications minister. The minister must then table a report in relation to that matter in both houses of parliament within seven sitting days of each house.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That is correct. But we haven't had an additional conversation with the ABC following the outcome of that report about what, if anything, they are prepared to do. So we haven't turned our mind to whether or not we need to make that recommendation. I think it's coordinated—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But the recommendation is not contingent on the ABC agreeing to what it's prepared to do.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Why weren't you able to do that as part of your inquiry in that 11-month period?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

text: Okay. I will try to move through these issues as quickly as I can. Can you please update the committee on your finalisation of the spectrum issues? I'm talking about the two-megahertz spectrum that is required by satellite providers in accordance with the UOMO legislation.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

text: Welcome back, Ms Inman Grant, and your team. I understand, Ms Inman Grant, this may be your last appearance in front of us as the eSafety Commissioner. That genuinely fills me with some sadness because I have enjoyed your appearances here enormously. You have been a very helpful witness to this committee in a range of different contexts. I won't say too much about it, but we are grateful for your service. I am personally very thankful for the way you've contributed to this committee's work.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Would you like to make an opening statement?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
I would, thank you. I would like to start by sharing my condolences to Helen Haines MP for the senseless attack she endured. My thoughts are with her, her family and her community. Chair and members, I would also like to acknowledge that this is a sensitive and pivotal moment for parliament. Over the past week, we've seen important public conversation about how online interactions can translate into real world harm. We've heard from current and former politicians across parliament. AFP commissioner Krissy Barrett has also drawn a direct link between inflammatory political discourse and threats against parliamentarians. The AFP commissioner and I spoke about these very issues in March.

I have been warning about the gravity of gendered online violence since 2018, when my office began seeing escalated abuse targeting women in the public eye cross politics, media, entertainment and sport. I saw this vile harassment firsthand at Twitter more than 15 years ago. What has become increasingly clear is that abuse manifests differently against women and girls than it does against men. It's sexualised. It's violent. It includes rape threats against the target and death threats against her children. It's physical—after her age, her appearance, her weight, her supposed virtue and even her fertility. It has a purpose—to silence women, to drive them from online spaces and, ultimately, out of public life.

Violent and targeted online abuse intended to cause serious harm is not a product of free expression. It is designed to suppress speech. This is precisely why parliament drew a line in 2021 around where online discourse becomes serious harm through the Adult Cyber Abuse Scheme. We've always been clear that the threshold is high. That means we can act as a safety net only after the most violent and egregious cases and after the harm has been done.

But, if we're honest, these regulatory tools do not reflect the way that abuse proliferates on platforms today. We've effectively been given a fly swatter to contain swarms of killer bees. That is why I looked to build other interventions, including the Women In The Spotlight program in 2018, to help women in the public eye manage online abuse more effectively. As online threats evolved, we knew women needed more tools to protect themselves so we expanded the program to include social media self-defence training, helping Australian women recognise emerging threats and how to build their psychological armour. Through this training, we also helped women assess whether online abuse could escalate into real-world harm and identify clear pathways to eSafety and police when threats become credible. We deliver bespoke eSafety webinars and face-to-face training, including with partners such as Pathways to Politics and Women for Election.

We also saw the next wave of gendered abuse coming. In 2020, our Tech Trends and Challenges program warned that deepfakes would disproportionately impact women and girls. They have. We worked with government to ensure that synthetic child sexual exploitation and deepfaked, image based sexual abuse were covered in our complaint schemes. We have a 96 per cent success rate in getting this devastating content taken down.

In eSafety Commissioner v Rotondo, we took action and we won against a particularly pernicious perpetrator who targeted women in this very chamber with deepfaked, image based sexual abuse. It sent a clear message: technology facilitated abuse cannot be committed with impunity. Cancel culture and vilification have made the environment dangerously febrile for women in senior government roles. When public officials are used for political point scoring, a target goes on our backs and we are subjected to an onslaught of online abuse and threats. Actions like this can have dangerous and escalating consequences for not just female politicians but also for senior government officials. As many of you know, this has been the normal state of affairs for me and my family for years. Somehow this is meant to be accepted as part of Public Service.

We need to do more for the next generation of leaders, who currently have little reason to feel safe or protected in online spaces or in public facing roles. Social media is no longer the once-envisioned digital town square. It has become more like a gladiatorial arena. Meanwhile, platforms continue to roll back abuse and violent speech policies that let some of the most egregious offenders out of digital jail. In this highly charged environment, our complaint schemes are not designed to operate at the velocity and scale at which abuse is hurled or to tackle the opaque algorithms amplifying it.

That is why I believe eSafety needs a range of interventions—a digital duty of care and stronger tools and protections for individuals, including a private right of action and legislation tailored to increasingly violent and threatening online hate. For example, in my witness statement to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, I proposed a targeted code aligned with the digital duty of care that could apply to caustic antisemitic content and other forms of online vilification. While broader reforms are considered, we will keep taking reports under our existing schemes and within the scope of our powers to help as many Australians as we can.

We know the vast majority of Australians want a safer internet, particularly for our children. That is exactly what eSafety was set up to deliver. Since our last estimates appearance, we have initiated several enforcement activities under the Online Safety Act and released new important educational resources. I would like to update the committee on that work.

Since June, three more AI-powered nudifying services have withdrawn their services from Australia following enforcement action through our online safety codes. In total, eight of the most widely used services have either withdrawn access from Australia or taken steps to comply with their obligations under the Online Safety Act. We commenced civil penalty proceedings in Federal Court against Telegram for its alleged failure to detect and remove pro-terror material from the platform. We secured court enforceable undertakings from Roblox to put in place robust measures to protect children from grooming, sexual exploitation and abuse. We used our transparency powers to expose what the world's largest online gaming service providers are and are not doing to protect users from serious online harms.

Alongside enforcement, prevention and education remain just as critical. Our Be Connected online digital literacy program for senior citizens has now reached three million users. We reached over 650,000 young men with lifesaving sexual extortion prevention messaging and support. In the last financial year, the eSafety website had 14.4 million visitors. Our webinars and digital campaigns reached four million Australians, including more than 1.7 million people through our trusted eSafety providers program.

We also released online safety advisories and new research sparking important conversations across the education community. This included research on AI chatbots and companions; guidance for parents on discussing the manosphere with their sons; practical guidance for schools on safely hosting student imagery in the age of AI; and advice on invasive technologies such as smart glasses.

In closing, it has been the honour of my professional life to serve as Australia's eSafety Commissioner for the past decade, leading the world's first online safety regulator and building the foundations for a stronger, innovative regulator ready for the challenges ahead. I will leave this role next year with deep respect for the Australians who come to us for help and immense pride in my staff, who meet that responsibility every day. Their tireless effort, commitment and passion for a mission have been unwavering. There has never been a more critical time for Australia to have a well-resourced online safety regulator with the right tools to tackle the much more complex and challenging world of AI. I look forward to discussing this with you and the committee and answering your questions. Thank you.

text:
You are the world's first eSafety Commissioner. You have undertaken an incredibly important role, mainly under our government. Of course, we appointed you in 2016. You were reappointed in 2022. I want to start by asking about the digital duty of care. Bear in mind that the bill itself is subject to a Senate inquiry. Obviously, I have participated in both a briefing with you and the department in relation to various aspects of what is proposed. One thing that has really concerned me, apart from all the free speech implications, is the removal of the codes and standards. They were removed completely in the exposure draft. It is now proposed that they will be removed after 12 months. The reason I am concerned about some of the narrative of the government in relation to the digital duty of care is that the codes and standards provide a whole range of important obligations on the platforms to take a whole range of actions, many of which are preventive—to prevent, detect and remove some of the most serious online harms. They cover not just the digital platforms. They cover ISPs, Internet search engine services, of course, messaging features and relevant electronic services—a wide range of obligations. Do you have concerns about the current proposal to remove the online codes and standards after 12 months?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

In our engagements with the department, as they were developing the digital duty of care, our concerns were always primarily with ensuring that there were very specific obligations placed on the platforms and that these were ultimately implementable and enforceable. We understood that this is a totally new and sweeping way to tackle these issues. The foundation is safety by design, which is something that we've been advocating for over years and years. I think we've come some way through our discussions, which the department touched on during the day. There have been many changes in the exposure draft. I think we're very comfortable with where we landed. Ms Snell, is there anything you want to add here?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
I think from our perspective it is a change. The codes and standards are prescriptive. The duty of care is a more general obligation. However, it is more futureproof because of the generality of that. It also provides significant obligations on to services up and down the tech stack in their obligation to undertake a risk assessment and to have appropriate and effective measures to address the risks they identify. That means that as you have emerging harms and they introduce new elements into their service, they are obligated to undertake a risk assessment before they introduce them.

At the moment—I think it is important to understand with the codes and standards—we still have to wait until something happens before we can take action against them. In fact, one of the biggest challenges with the codes is that we have to give them a direction to comply before we can take enforcement action.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Ms Snell, that's not quite accurate. The codes and standards also include preventive measures that platforms must take to prevent, detect and remove very seriously unlawful online material.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But for us to establish that they haven't done that, we need to identify that content on their service. The difference with the risk assessment is that if they identify the possibility of that being on their service, they have to also provide specific mitigation measures to deal with that. At the moment, we find that we have to wait until certain material—for example, child sexual exploitation material—is being posted on a platform. More accurately, let's take the example we have in court, where we have to have found pro-terror content on the Telegram service. We can then take them to court for the fact that they don't have appropriate systems and processes in place to have kept that off.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, that would be a direct breach of their obligations to detect and remove.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator, do you have the response to 694?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Generally—this is what happened with some of the more recent footage, for example, in the Charlie Kirk shooting—we issue removal notices and we accept geo-blocking as substantive compliance with those notices. That's our general position for illegal and restricted content. It's a different position. We might issue removal notices for child sexual abuse material, for example. It does depend on the material. Generally for illegal and illustrative content, we do accept geo-blocking.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. It's just that sort of illegal content can still be accessed here in Australia. Is that an enforceability power that you would need? Where is the gap there? portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There are challenges with overseas offshore entities that do not have any presence here in Australia and choose not to submit to the jurisdiction here in Australia. I'm not sure that there's even an easy legislative fix for that. If a recalcitrant third party offshore does not want to comply, there are limitations on what further action we can take in those circumstances. So we issue removal notices. A lot of services actually respond to them. In this case, sometimes the service chooses not to do that. In some instances, we can engage with the AFP to exercise blocking it at an ISP level. The challenge we see with that is often that URLs are simply changed and the material is made available again. So it is a challenge.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's also possible to go upstream to the hosting providers. But if it's a really bad site, they generally choose hosting providers that are also in permissive hosting environments and are non-responsive.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I see impossibility stacked on top of impossibility. I think we discussed it in the draft answer to SQ26-000696. Fines or core action against the US government is all but prohibited by the Foreign States Immunities Act. Is that the case here? Is that what we're up against?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're up against a broad range of permissive hosting environments. It's not any one geography or government. It is a lot of bad actors, unfortunately. Again, we use the tools that we can to try to go upstream. But we also have other tools where we can try to disrupt or minimise accessibility. That's through the search engine deindexing power. We do use the tools that we have, but we are working in a global environment. It's worth noting that, I think in the 10 years I have been in this role, we've only had one instance where child sexual abuse has been hosted in Australia because we've had such strong laws on the books for almost a quarter of a century. There are still so many developed and advanced countries around the globe and those in the global south that do not have similar laws so anything goes. That's what we're up against.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

Obviously, we've got finite resources. There's a lot of illegal content on the Internet. We need to focus where it's most likely that Australians are going to interact with that content.

If we want to get into what the words might mean in a legislative sense, we can answer those questions for you in more detail during the Senate inquiry. I don't have the bill in front of me. I'm not sure whether there is a particular legislative definition of that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: For clarity, eSafety do not currently have any researchers or personnel operating overseas?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We do not. They are all located in either Canberra, Sydney or Melbourne.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There is nothing going forward that might require them to operate overseas?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No plans to.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That is an appropriate time to take our dinner break. We will return with the eSafety Commissioner. Thank you very much.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We will resume our session with the eSafety Commissioner. Senator Henderson.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Commissioner, could you update the committee on the social media ban and any updated statistics that you have as to the success or otherwise of the measure? I have some other questions to ask on this as well.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: As you will recall, there was a legislative amendment that provided us with significant new powers. That went to an inquiry. That reached royal assent on a Friday afternoon. The following Monday, when we were able to do so, we started issuing notices. So we're really in the thick of going back and forth with about five companies and all their lawyers in getting these notices. We're starting to get them in and collate them. I would just say that we're deep in the regulatory investigations process. Ms Snell or Mr Fleming, would you like to add anything?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I was actually seeking updated data on compliance with the social media ban.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator, we've moved now to two-monthly reporting on numbers rather than monthly. We don't have the latest responses from the platforms because we have focused our notice powers really on getting information and documents under the new powers to progress the investigations. That is because the numbers no longer really tell us the story of whether platforms are complying. Those numbers now take into account a whole range of things that makes it difficult to use them to assess compliance. Our inquiries now tend to focus more on, particularly in terms of documents, what systems and processes and policies they have in place and their decision-making around compliance. They go to the heart of the investigations.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Commissioner, are you saying that previously you have reported on the number of under-16 teenagers who are still able to access a social media account?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Are you saying that you are no longer reporting on that?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We had a separate evaluation, a longitudinal evaluation, where we're providing research and getting data from about 4,000 dyads—parents and children. We put the first evaluation out there. We collected in May. That is where we found that there was a 20 per cent decrease in holdings of under-16s having accounts. There were some other interesting and notable trends. As you know, we're trying to look at everything from whether they are sleeping better or playing more sport and whether they are being asked by the platforms to even age assure. Fifty per cent of children told us at that time they had not. So we're doing these in three-month increments. Of course, three months is early to see market changes. I believe we just hit the six-month mark and are collating the data from that. We will be able to provide something later this year.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I am a bit confused here. You are doing three-monthly reporting on compliance?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. This is really the evaluation of what kind of impacts the policy and the implementation are having on a broad range of factors.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Shouldn't there be a report for the end of September? When was the most recent report?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There's a distinction between other compliance and enforcement reporting notices that Ms Snell referred to. That happens now every second month. The commissioner is referring to our long-term evaluation, where we released one report. We have another report coming out before the end of the year. That is exploring the impact of the policy on the lives of Australians, not the compliance numbers from platforms.
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. When is that report due?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The evaluation report or the compliance report?
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The compliance report.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: At this stage, we are not putting out another public compliance report like the March one because we are in in-depth investigations. We consider that reporting at this point may prejudice those investigations. So the outcome of those investigations will be our next public reporting in terms of the platforms' compliance.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The March compliance report showed that seven out of 10 children under the age of 16 were still on social media. That was your assessment. Why is that not important to continue to report on, Commissioner?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're continuing using the tools that we have to be able to ask those questions. We're taking multiple approaches that gives us a much broader range of data. Of course it's important, but anything that will undermine the integrity of an investigation is something that we have to deeply consider.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Commissioner, how is informing Australians about the success or otherwise of the social media ban undermining integrity? Surely part of your job is to be transparent.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Absolutely. We didn't need to do this evaluation to try to look at things such as the impact on schooling and sleep and even unintended consequences. The other thing we can tell you that we're continuing to track is the speculation that young people would be migrating to darker areas of the Internet. We haven't seen any evidence of that. In fact, it shows you how entrenched the power of these mainstream social media companies has been. When underage children started going to places like Bigo Live, Lemon8 or CapCut and downloaded, we might have seen temporary spikes. But they never really used the platforms because there wasn't a critical mass of their peers there. We're seeing kids reconvening where their friends are, and that's mostly on messaging sites and on group text.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Could I also just clarify—
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry. There is the social media minimum age compliance update of March 2026. When was the decision made not to do any more compliance updates?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When we moved into more formal investigations following the issuing of that compliance update, the decision was made to focus on the detailed investigations and preserve the integrity of those investigations to ensure that we are best placed to take enforcement action against companies for non-compliance once we finished our evidence gathering.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Isn't it also important that Australians know the success or otherwise of this law?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I could clarify. The seven out of 10 statistic you mentioned actually came from a research survey, not from the compliance notices. We are continuing to capture that data through research and evaluation methods. The elements that Ms Snell is referring to are around the investigation.
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I know the difference.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I know it was from a research survey.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The one in March as well.
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You haven't rung every child under the age of 16.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But we did not get that information from notices from platforms, just to clarify.
witness_position: General Manager, Corporate and Strategy Group

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I understand it. I'm talking about the compliance update. I'm just raising concerns that there has been a decision made not to continue to do those reports.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We do have a small number of staff. The same staff are doing all the assessments of the notices, writing the notices and helping us build the evidence for the case. We have a research team that is doing the evaluations separately. These are all mixed methods. At some point we also have to prioritise where we need to focus our efforts. I think what Ms Snell was saying is that our priority, given that we know compliance is not what it should be, is gathering the evidence that we can take to court that they are not taking reasonable steps to keep under-16s from having and holding accounts. This is what you have to do as a small regulator. You have to balance. We thought the March report was very important, but it was a huge and heavy lift.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Commissioner, can you update me on your investigation? Minister Wells did an interview where she was asked if you were suing Facebook, TikTok and other platforms. She indicated yes but then added a condition to her answer. Could you please provide an update as to where you are at? Are you suing these platforms? Will you be commencing proceedings?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: If we have the evidence to make a case. Again, we have about a six-month lag because of the inquiry that went on in terms of getting those new powers—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. That's not true, Commissioner.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, Minister. The proposal was the middle of the year. There was about a two-month period—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
I'm talking about from the beginning when we first realised where we were and the tools that we didn't have and raised it with the government. That whole process took about six months. The moment we got the powers we started using them. We are asking them extensive questions. We're actually dealing with relatively new assurance providers who haven't dealt with lawyers and who haven't been part of document processes. We're doing lots of back and forth. We're gathering all the evidence that we can. Obviously, we are looking at the potential outcome of the High Court challenge. We're going to see how that plays out in November. That could ultimately have bearing on costs depending on the outcomes. So we're looking at a number of factors. I will go back to what Ms Snell said to you. We are deep in the throes of trying to build the evidence to put some key cases together. There may be some cases. Obviously, the litigation in the US was significant. They are asking for different things, or it goes further in some respects from just having and holding accounts. We are having conversations with the platforms. In any geography, we would expect that, if they are taking some safety interventions in one major market, they will do the same here.

We have a range of different enforcement actions we could be looking at. They may come in different forms depending on how well each respective company is doing on compliance and improving compliance and based on whether or not it will require enforcement action in the courts. Something like an enforceable undertaking might be more appropriate. It is wherever we get the best outcome in terms of lifting that compliance.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So you've issued notices and production of document notices to which organisations?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The five companies that we announced in March that we are investigating. We have also sent—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: For the purposes of these proceedings, could you name those five companies?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: TikTok, Snap, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube. We've also issued notices to a number of the third-party age assurance providers that they are using, including k-ID and Yoti. We've also issued notices to the app stores, including Google Play and the Apple iTunes store. Both of them, as you would recall, have recently issued age range APIs, which provides the companies with specific signals. We want to understand what kind of contractual arrangements there might be there or across the board.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Commissioner, on notice, could we have a full list of all those companies to which you have issued notices? Could we also please have copies of the notices and any responses you've received as well?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not sure.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We can take it on notice, Senator. As we've discussed before, these are investigation processes underway. We need to protect the integrity of our investigation. In considering what we can provide in response to the question on notice, we'll consider whether or not we need to make a public interest immunity claim over that material.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Alright. Thank you very much. I appreciate that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Henderson, I need to share the call.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I have a final couple of very quick questions. Commissioner, as you know, I have raised ongoing concerns about the public statements of both the Prime Minister and the communications minister as to the number of social media accounts that have been shut down, discontinued and suspended. It started off at 4.7 million. The latest declaration from the Prime Minister is over six million. I have raised concerns that the Prime Minister and the communications minister continue to mislead Australians in relation to this figure. As I have ascertained, and as I've said very openly and publicly, at least several million of that total relates to Google accounts which have nothing to do with YouTube. They are Google accounts, because YouTube does not have a separate account. For instance, if you want to have Gmail, you need a Google account. I am concerned that those numbers are seriously inflated because of the way in which the data has been collated. It is misrepresenting to Australians the number of accounts that have actually been closed down. Can you please update the committee on that issue? It is a burning issue. I'm not going to give up on it, Commissioner. I would like and ask that you be transparent about those numbers, please.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We provided a great deal of transparency, I believe, in the in-camera session. You are right in saying that YouTube is anomalous in terms of how they capture accounts or deactivations because of the nature of Google accounts. I think we account for those in terms of the lexicon we use. We say removed or deactivated because that is the terminology the companies provided us.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: At least several million of these accounts have nothing to do with social media accounts. Gmail has nothing to do with a prohibited social media account. I am only saying this because you have just given that evidence. You did provide extensive further information in camera. I would be very keen for you to provide that information openly, please, so we can put this issue to rest. I don't like the fact that the Prime Minister and the communications minister continue to use these inflated numbers which mislead Australians.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I think that we have not provided that information publicly on the basis of public interest immunity. That has not been overturned at this time.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Have you made a public interest immunity claim?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry? In relation to the individual numbers for each platform?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. Have you made a public interest immunity claim, Mr Fleming?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When it was originally asked.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. You have not made a public interest immunity claim.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There are questions on notice we had from one round of Senate estimates.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Fleming—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We'll check on that, Senator.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It has not been a matter that has come to our committee. You have indicated that you did not answer the question earlier because it was a matter under investigation.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I ask you, Commissioner, in your final estimates if you could please apprise this committee of the breakdown of those numbers so that we can understand. We know there are 550,000 Facebook accounts. I'm rattling them off from the top of my head. It is slightly less than that for Instagram. The numbers don't add up. I ask that you provide a breakdown, as you did in camera.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I don't have those numbers in front of me. We'll have to take it on notice.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We'll need to take it on notice because we don't have those numbers here. Senator, what I can say is that it's not correct to say that the number of Google accounts is not related to social media. The step that Google took was to prevent Google accounts for underage users from being able to access YouTube, so it was directly relevant to the fact that YouTube is an age restricted social media platform.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. That's not correct, Ms Snell. It's very difficult to have this conversation when we've had extensive evidence in camera. The number of deactivated accounts included young children who just had a Gmail account. They were only—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What was deactivated was their access to YouTube.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Their Gmail account wasn't deactivated or their overall Google account wasn't deactivated. Their ability to access YouTube was prevented.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. But that number was included in the overall figure, including those—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Because those young people are no longer able to access YouTube.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It is prevented from having and holding an account, yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's right. So there were several million young Australians who held a Google account because they were just using Google for Gmail. As we know, you don't need to log in to YouTube to watch YouTube. So it's actually very hard—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It was a feature of the bill that you could watch those in a logged-out state.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I appreciate that. You have taken that on notice. I would be really grateful if we could finalise this matter.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you for appearing again. In the most recent period you have data for, what amount of child sexual abuse material, revenge porn, deep fakes and similar material has the eSafety Commissioner removed from the web? I'm not talking about violent extremist or political material. I'm talking about what has always been the core responsibility of your office—protecting children.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Over what period, Senator?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: In your most recent period.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That would be 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. In terms of illegal and restricted content, which represents about 39 per cent of our reports, there were 27,581 complaints received. Those, of course, we work through the INHOPE network to get rapid removal within three days. That was successful in terms of image based abuse. We don't refer to it as revenge porn. Colloquially, it is the same thing. We had about 9,041 reports representing 37 per cent. Where we had a real jump in reports was in the adult cyberabuse area. There was an increase of about 57 per cent. There were 5,718. To round it off, our youth cyberbullying scheme had 3,688 reports.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. What stands out is a marked increase in adult cyberabuse?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Are deep fakes still a thing?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Synthetic content and deep faked image-based abuse are, as a result of the 2021 Online Safety Act, all covered. Again, the most manifestations we're seeing of deep faked or manipulated images is through the Image-Based Abuse Scheme. We still have a 96 per cent success rate in getting that taken down. There has to be a sexualised component to it, however.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: How have deep fakes evolved, if at all, in the age of AI?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: How have deep fakes evolved in the age of AI?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Six years ago, it was much more technologically difficult to achieve a credible deep fake. It required hundreds of different images from different angles of a single person's face, a lot of computing power and technical expertise. Now you can use a nudifying service, where you upload an image, or you can use an app. Within seconds you can get credible deep fakes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. What cooperation are you getting from international law enforcement and big tech to take this material down? I note generally increasing organisation and cooperation on these matters. Is that correct?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. We've had success using our codes and standards. We've been able to ensure that eight overseas nudifying services are either no longer providing their services into Australia or are complying now with our age restricted material codes and applying age assurance technologies. Those eight companies accounted for about 200,000 downloads per month by Australians.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you. What percentage of your staff or operational budget is taken up by these activities, your original core duties, rather than the other areas taking up your time, which is extremist or violent material?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We've got about 36 investigators out of about 250 individuals.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Dealing with complaints.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Dealing with the complaints, and an investigation stream.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have additional investigators under our codes and standards, which have been responsible for the nudify app actions.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So your core business is looking after children and other threats. So you are achieving results there still. We praise your office for that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We really appreciate that, Senator Roberts. We were just talking about the fact that because we have the codes and standards, that covers a broad range across the technology stack. Even if you look at the designated Internet services, there are probably millions of sites that we're talking about. We're talking about how overall we're regulating hundreds and thousands of different technologies and platforms. By necessity, we have to prioritise high-risk, high-harm interventions. Of course, that involves children experiencing sexual abuse and anything like sexual extortion, which can happen to both young men or children. Sadistic sexual extortion is happening more to young girls as young as nine or 10 years old. Image abused abuse, which also has a sexualised component, has to be our top priority.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I have also been consistent with the next issue that I raise. That is what many people, including me, see as a power grab. In this case, it may not just be the eSafety Commissioner. It may be the government. I will explain. There is a confluence between the protection measures you admirably pursue, such as child sexual abuse material, and the new digital duty of care bill. This is in part the ability to create sock puppet accounts. I will use an example. There is AI somewhere generating realistic child porn. Is that correct?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I don't understand how those people are not immediately caught and prosecuted, let alone the AI being trained not to produce that material. This is a problem, right?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, it is a problem. It's a problem to prove a specific application or service. For instance, at the end of December last year, it was alleged that Grok had been used to generate child sexual abuse material as well as image based abuse of adults. We have observed that as some of those images tend to go viral, the watermarking and indications about whether or not those came from Grok tend to degrade. The ability to have test accounts and test whether you can adversarially convince one of these platforms to generate that is an issue. Sorry, I'm not sure I can talk just now.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We will briefly suspend and wait a minute.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We'll recommence. Senator Roberts?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You could use the sock puppet power to create a fake account yourself and test out the capability of AI to produce that material or deep fakes, for that matter, and, if successful, prosecute them. There aren't that many AI companies. Is there any other way to achieve that same objective without sock puppets?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
Test accounts, research accounts or what are colloquially referred to as sock puppet accounts are pretty commonly used tools by regulators. The idea is that right now we send notices that give us answers. One of the only ways we can test the claims is by testing them ourselves. I will give you three examples of how we would like to be able to use these tests now. With the social media ban, they are providing us notice and we are doing research. The only way we can really test how well calibrated the triggers are for each platform is when we're setting up an account as a 13-year-old to see whether or not the age assurance is triggered. That will tell us whether or not it is working accurately or give us an indication.

Another example is the one that you put forward. You can't prove in a court of law necessarily from a set of images that application produced them unless you do some adversarial testing and you provide them prompts to try to get them to create child sexual abuse. Once you have that evidence, you can bring it into a court of law.

The third example would be what we actually had to do with respect to Roblox. We asked them to put 10 significant safety protections into place, including preventing adult accounts from contacting child accounts without explicit parental consent. They said they had done that. We used what we called avowed accounts. We told them that we were doing that. We tested to see if the parental consent was being triggered in the way that it should. We were not satisfied. What is interesting is that when you are an avowed account, they can obviously, through intrusion detection, see that you are in their systems. It means that they can clean up and change things as you go along. You want to be able to test in a way that they are not trying to change things as you go along so you know how their features, systems and processes work in practice. You want that confidence when a child is undergoing the same actions that they are going to get a consistent safety response.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So in every scenario we've heard to justify sock puppet accounts their use is limited in time. Seven days seems to be the longest it would be needed. Ms Inman Grant or the minister, could you have included in the digital duty of care provision to only operate sock puppets for limited periods and published the name and use of the account on a public register on a monthly or quarterly basis post op so the public can have confidence you are using the powers as intended and not running a propaganda exercise under the guise of public safety? That would restore confidence, wouldn't it?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, Senator, this is a question for government. Just for the record, this is about testing systems and processes. This is not about individuals. It is not about surveillance. There is no precedent that we have set. We have never—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It may not be with you, but it could be in future.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. Well—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's not just okay. That terrifies people.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Of course. I understand that. I think if you look at the current bill vis- -vis the exposure draft, you see that some of it requires transparency reporting. This again is a question for government. If it gave you greater comfort that there was a purpose limitation for these kinds of testing, I'm sure we could work through that too.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, the problem seems to be intent. Many people across Australia see it as a way to control and suppress everyday Australians. There is a lack of tight definitions of destructive behaviour. There is a lack of responsibility on people who post as well as people who distribute. In other words, if I post something nasty or offensive, it should be on me—my responsibility—as well as the platform I'm using for distributing it. It should be on both. These are things that indicate to people that the intent is to control.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Can you provide me with the evidence of that earlier supposition you made about surveillance? We're not a law enforcement agency, an intelligence agency or a national security agency.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They are very concerned after the COVID response about government control of people.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: About broad government control?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Broad government control that can be used by a future government to create evil.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That is why I think a purpose limitation that is very specific could give a degree of comfort.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Based on behaviours. I think the cat is out of the bag now.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts, I will need to share the call in a moment.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. I will come back.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts, if it assists you, the bill is obviously before the committee. There will be an inquiry into the bill. You can ask more questions. We will get a chance to respond to some of those points.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Minister, you would be aware that many people are deeply concerned, especially after the first draft that was taken back.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator, I will not get into the views right now. I will not respond in a full way about what I think is happening online, which I would characterise as misinformation about what is actually in and isn't in the bill. For you and I to have a full discussion about that, we would probably need to do that in another forum. What I will say is that there is a Senate inquiry that the chair is going to handle. We will be able to explore the bill in a fuller way through that process. I'm sure there will be a parliamentary debate as well.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. The key point I have made is responsibility.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not in a debate with you about this, Senator. I think the chair is actually—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not after solutions now.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I am saying that you are wrong.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It would be very helpful—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, let's have a talk.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: if the intent of the bill and the actual provisions were discussed instead of some conspiracy theory about freedom of speech.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Now you're labelling me.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, Senator. I am very concerned that there is some ill-intent in the way that—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, let's have a talk.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sure. That would be great. Thanks. We can get you a briefing on the bill, if you like.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, please.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Wonderful.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm trying to think of a term apart from 'sock puppet'. An assumed identity.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: A testing account.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: A testing account. It is common practice in Europe for researchers to have testing accounts and largely to hold these big, otherwise unaccountable, platforms to account. They go on to the account and test if what they are saying is true—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Exactly.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: to determine what the experience is, for example, for a 16-year-old. They may not be 16. It is to see if the asserted protections in place for a 16-year-old are actually in place and to test these platforms in real time. They have been critically important to holding these platforms to account, particularly with researchers and agencies and in Europe, haven't they?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Absolutely. I think we're past the stage of asking a question and they give us an answer and we take them at their word. They are not going to prove it and demonstrate it through technical means. We are a regulator in an increasingly opaque environment. You know very well that many of these platforms are becoming more opaque rather than more transparent. In the age and complexity of AI, we're absolutely going to be able to need to adversarially test the prompts. I don't know if you saw the Tech against terrorism report that recently came out. It talked about the obliteration of safeguards from open weight models in as little as three days.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So, as I understand it, the digital duty of care bill puts in place a whole series of quite limited purposes for these assumed identities. It ensures that there is reporting on it. It is one of the most critical ways that millions of Australians can have some kind of confidence or actually some kind of transparency over the assertions that these big platforms make. They say that they put protections in for young people, and often they are not there. They make assertions about someone's journey through the platform, and they are often false. Unless you can put something in to test it, you are relying upon platforms that, in my experience, have proven utterly untrustworthy. That is ultimately the intent behind this, isn't it?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Absolutely. Professor Laura Edelson's report Broken, buried, or missing reports on tests of 80 different safety features. If they were to be believed, it is that they are all working as planned or could be discoverable. This is kind of the game that is played, sadly. I am thinking of an example. Instagram came tell us that they were removing likes. There was a big fanfare made about it. I don't know the amount of time—whether it was a month or a year—but all of a sudden the likes were back. There was no communication about that or explanation.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
For those politicians who trust Meta, for those politicians who trust Elon Musk, for those politicians who trust big tech, maybe they don't want this. Maybe they are quite happy having big tech self-regulate and make untested assertions. I can tell you now that my party believes there needs to be a way to not just trust but to verify. We can see a rationale behind this.

Could I ask you a matter that's been raised with me by a number of people who pretty much love online gaming, and it's what Steam has been doing about introducing a new age-verification system that is limited to credit cards. Last time I checked, barely half of Australian adults had credit cards, and almost no kids had credit cards. This is said to be for an age-verification purpose, but what it's meant is that so many gamers can't get access to Steam, can't get their updates, can't get their games. Are you challenging? Are you pushing back against Steam? This seems an unreasonable requirement.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, we agree, and we think it doesn't meet the fairness bar that it has laid out in the [inaudible] terms. You may have seen that we did a much more comprehensive transparency report around a number of online gaming systems. We looked at Roblox. We looked at Minecraft. We looked at Fortnite, as part of Epic Games, and then Valve and Steam. Valve and Steam definitely had fewer safety interventions than the rest.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Steam have said though—they've put you in it. They've said, 'This is because what eSafety has demanded.'

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They also were not a part of any of the development of the codes throughout that process, and really the only one of those companies—all they had to do is read the guidance that the gaming industry themselves built. We have reached out to them. We've told them that we think it's problematic and that people are effectively blocked from being able to use their platforms. They said they will be looking at alternative methods, but they didn't give us specific dates as to when that will be.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Are there any actions you can take, given it doesn't appear to be meeting the accessibility and reasonableness provisions in the code? What actions can you take if Steam don't change their position and allow people to find other more reasonable ways to prove identity?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: If they don't—as the commissioner said, we have been engaging with them, and they have committed to explore further methods of age assurance. We'll continue to engage with them at this stage. If they don't, then there are a range of options which we would need to consider as part of that. As a first step, under the codes, we can issue a direction to comply, so, if we were to form a formal view—which I would say we haven't formally formed a view that they're not compliant yet because we're still engaging with them. If we were to form that view, then we could look to issue a direction to comply, and, if they then didn't take further steps, then we would look to enforcement action. Obviously, that is then subject to legal advice.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's causing a lot of anxiety, if the quantity of concerns being raised with my office is any indication. Could I ask you, Commissioner, to have some ongoing public reporting about where this is up to with Steam so there's some transparency about it? It's creating not just frustration but genuine anxiety amongst people.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. I'm happy to do that. I don't think we put any time restrictions on them, but we've given them notice. We've given them our—I just want to make sure that any communication is fair and is—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not putting any parameters.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: If we were to conduct an investigation, we would need to think about how much we would say publicly.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not putting parameters around what you can say. If you're in the process of an investigation, there may be reasons you keep some of that confidential. If you're having productive, confidential discussions with Steam, you may keep some of that confidential, but as much information as you can reasonably provide would be very helpful for people, because there's a lot of concern about it.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We can provide relevant updates to your office as things develop.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That would be that would also be helpful so we could respond. Going back onto the duty of care, some of the key addictive elements the platforms have are things like autoscroll, autoplay and endless scroll—that addictive design. Do you have a view about whether the concept of addictive design or problematic overuse is going to be effectively addressed in the digital duty of care? They're not expressly put in the bill. Do you see a way in which they will be potentially adequately addressed in the bill?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I think those are policy questions that will eventually need to come out through the inquiry process. It's broad. I would say to you, if that is a concern and you would like to see something more explicit, do raise that with the government. I think it's a legitimate concern.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I might raise it with the Senate.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I was just reflecting on the AI inquiry. Kate Chaney asked some very important questions about how to tackle things. We're talking about sycophancy and anthropomorphism in the context of AI chatbots, but what about emotional attachment? How do you use regulatory tools beyond prevention to prevent that happening? Again, I think it would probably require more testing in terms of looking at source code if we arrived at the opinion that it was harmful not just for young people but for people more broadly in terms of how these chat bots are programmed to further suck people in.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Could I ask three quick things on the digital duty of care?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, but before you do, I think I've been a bit indulgent at this point, given the way I've enforced these rules, particularly against Senator Henderson, which is to say—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I had very strict—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I was going to stand up for you, Senator Henderson.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I was just waiting to politely interject.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I appreciate the politeness in the room. Essentially the advice I've received and the proposition I set out at the front is we really can't go to the substance of the digital duty of care here today while it's subject to a Senate inquiry. It is about process and administration.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay, I get it. I accept that. Pretend I didn't say, 'digital duty of care', then!

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm afraid that bell has been rung!

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Given the time, I might try and find another way of progressing some matters.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I don't want you to try and find a way of rewording them in order to achieve the same outcome.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I won't do a ruse. I hear your ruling, and I understand it. We're bound by it, so it's not a problem. Can I ask you about paid advertising and the extent to which paid advertising relies upon gathering data, sometimes tracking people's physical location, quite often tracking what people are browsing on, building up a data picture about potential customers and then, having built up that picture about potential customers, selling that as a product to advertisers. Do you have any concerns as eSafety Commissioner about that practice and about how it allows potential noxious players to profile young people, to profile women, to identify targets for potential harassment or other mischief?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I have concern about dodgy practices like that. I think that falls probably more under the purview of the Privacy Commissioner. There are other questions around advertising that I think are germane to online safety; we might not have a nexus in current legislation or even in the future. One of those is the fact that mainstream social media companies and search engines that make advertising revenue are advertising CSAM and nudifying apps. That is concerning to me. The other thing that's concerning to me is that we know they have the technology to target you with deadly precision with advertising down to your child's school shoes and their classroom, yet they can't seem to identify the age of the child; that's too hard. When I think about the targeting technologies that they have for advertising not being applied to these other challenges, I find that quite frustrating.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
They can identify my age, they seem to work out where I'm about to go on holiday, they seem to know if I'm hungry, but they can't determine if someone's 16 or 17. These things don't seem to logically follow. Perhaps that's why we need the ability to go beyond their assertions and put researchers in to find out the truth.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have been following migratory patterns through market intelligence tools, as well as through our comprehensive longitudinal evaluation.
