portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

text: Welcome, Ms Sweeney and members of your team at the table and in the room. Do you wish to make an opening statement?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
I do. Chair, thank you to you and to the members of the committee. Before I start, if I may, I would like to acknowledge the devastating and deeply troubling attack on Dr Helen Haines. Like so many Australians, at NBN we were shocked and deeply concerned by what occurred, and our thoughts are with Dr Haines, her family, her colleagues and everyone impacted by this incredibly distressing incident. Dr Haines is a passionate advocate for regional communities and for ensuring regional Australians can access the connectivity and the opportunities across Australia, and at NBN we greatly value her advocacy and her commitment to regional communications.

As we turn to today's and tonight's proceedings, it is a privilege to be back here before the committee to provide an update on NBN's progress. At the heart of everything we do at NBN is our purpose, and our purpose is to elevate Australia by connecting people and by powering progress. That purpose is reflected in the progress we have made this year. We have strengthened the network and expanded access to more reliable and faster broadband, and we are building the digital infrastructure that Australia will rely on, we think and we know, for decades to come.

FY26, the financial year, was a successful year for NBN. In an increasingly competitive environment, we delivered strong operational and financial results. We accelerated the transition from legacy copper technologies to more reliable, future-ready fibre and continued to lift the capability and resilience of the network.

Today I'd like to cover three key things with the committee: the outcomes we delivered in financial year 26, the growing momentum behind Australia's transition from legacy copper to fibre and the work underway to strengthen network resilience as we prepare for the upcoming high-risk weather season. FY26 was a year of excellent progress for NBN, and it was reinforced by the ACCC's final replacement determination, which was released on 27 August this year. The determination represents a landmark regulatory outcome for NBN, and it provides regulatory certainty for FY27-29. It effectively validated 100 per cent of NBN's forecast capital and operating expenditure as prudent and efficient. The ACCC also concluded that close to 99 per cent of NBN's historical capex—and that was across FY24-26—met the same standard. Together, these findings provide strong, independent validation of NBN's strategy, investment framework and long-term approach to network modernisation.

Against that backdrop, we met or exceeded key FY26 financial guidance targets. By way of highlights, total revenue grew three per cent, and that was to $5.92 billion; our EBITDA grew five per cent, to $4.46 billion; telecommunications revenue grew by four per cent, to $5.75 billion—that was supported by the adoption of higher speed tiers; and operating costs, I think importantly, reduced by $52 million or three per cent. That reflects the disciplined cost management and the growing benefits of transitioning Australians from that legacy copper to full fibre.

At the same time, we continued to accelerate our fibre rollout. In FY26, we upgraded more than 575,000 premises—homes and businesses, rather—from copper to fibre, and that's a 34 per cent uplift on the previous year. We reached 3.3 million premises on our fibre network, and that's a 24 per cent increase on the previous year. This marked a clear inflection point, with more customers connected to fibre than copper for the first time in NBN's history. Those results demonstrate an important point. As more Australians benefit from more reliable, faster services, the nation gains a more capable and more resilient asset.

To my second point, accelerating Australia's move to fibre, the momentum behind Australia's transition from copper to fibre continues to strengthen. It's now been one year since we launched Accelerate Great, the most significant uplift in NBN's high-speed wholesale tiers since the network was established. The customer response has been strong. At the end of FY26, 47 per cent of customers were on a hundred megabits and above, and that's up from 32 per cent the year before. Thirty-seven per cent of customers were on 500 megabits or above, and that is up from four per cent the previous year. Today, around 3.5 million premises are connected to 500 megabits and above, and that's making, for the first time, the 500-megabit plan the most popular speed tier on the NBN network. Fibre is underpinning this shift. It's delivering more reliable, more resilient and faster connectivity with capacity to support the growing digital data demands, including more connected devices, cloud services and emerging technologies such as AI.

That demand is already increasing. By the end of September, average monthly downloads had increased by 14 per cent year on year, while average monthly uploads had increased by 18 per cent. Together, these trends demonstrate that Australians are consuming, creating and sharing more data. It's reinforcing the importance of continued investment in high-capacity broadband infrastructure, and this will be even more important as AI, cloud computing, real-time collaboration and other data-intensive applications place greater demands on the network performance and on reliability and resilience.

Access to world-class digital infrastructure will be an important enabler of Australia's future productivity and economic growth, and fibre provides the reliability, the capacity and the upgrade path required to support that growth across regional and metropolitan Australia. Over the past four years, NBN has undertaken one of the largest digital infrastructure upgrades in Australia's history. We've transformed the capability of the network. In 2022, just 46 per cent of fixed line premises could access wholesale speeds of one gigabit. Today, 90 per cent of homes and businesses can order a highly reliable multigigabit service, and once the remaining copper fibre footprint has been upgraded, more than 11.6 million homes and businesses, representing around 94 per cent of the fixed line footprint, will be able to access multigigabit capable services. Importantly—and I think this is very important—this capability will extend well beyond our cities, reaching 99 per cent of regional fixed line premises by 2030.

The final step in achieving that outcome is the upgrade of the remaining 622,000 premises served by legacy copper on our fibre-to-the-node technology, where we continue to make strong progress, and we remain on track to make all eligible premises ready for a fibre upgrade by the end of 2030. At the end of September of this year, 95 per cent of that footprint had progressed to detailed designs, 48 per cent are now in construction, and more than 100,000 of that 622,000 are now ready to order a fibre upgrade. Another important milestone was achieved on 1 July this year, when fibre-to-the-kerb customers on legacy copper technology became eligible to upgrade to fibre without needing to subscribe to higher speed wholesale plans. This is helping Australia's acceleration and that migration away from ageing legacy copper infrastructure. Building on this change, NBN is progressively removing similar wholesale tier eligibility requirements across the remaining fibre-to-the-node upgrade footprint, with implementation planned for March of 2027.

The objective is simple: make it easier for Australians to access the benefits of full fibre. Customers are increasingly choosing fibre because it delivers what modern households and businesses need most: more capacity, lower latency, greater reliability and a superior broadband experience. And as more Australians move to fibre, we are seeing fewer faults, fewer technician visits and better community resilience. At the same time, fibre is improving network economics, driving capital efficiency and helping us build a stronger, more resilient Australian broadband network. So, whether measured through upgrade volume, higher speed tier adoption, data consumption or customer behaviour, the direction is clear: Australians are choosing fibre and, once connected, they are increasingly choosing more reliable and faster services.

Finally, to my last point, resilience remains central to our purpose, and as we approach another high-risk weather season, NBN has undertaken extensive preparations to help Australians remain connected before, during and after severe weather events. This includes prepositioning generators, fuel supplies, satellite trucks, flyaway satellite kits, temporary network restoration equipment and specialist field resources in identified risk areas. We also continue to work closely with emergency management agencies, utilities and government stakeholders to coordinate the response and recovery arrangements. A key component of this preparation is EM365. That's our year-round preparedness and resilience program. Through EM365, we provide customers with practical preparedness information, outage notifications, multilingual resources and guidance to help households, businesses and communities prepare for emergency and maintain communications during times of disruption. Importantly, resilience is not only how we respond during severe weather events; it's also about how we continue to strengthen the network itself.

Again, as we've mentioned previously, as more customers transition from legacy copper to fibre, they benefit from an infrastructure that is inherently more resilient, with fewer points of failure, less reliance on powered infrastructure in the field and faster restoration following major weather events. Fibre now represents the majority of active fixed line connections. It's improving reliability and resilience while reducing operational complexity and strengthening network economics. As communities, businesses and government services become increasingly dependent on digital connectivity, the importance of a reliable, resilient national network will continue to grow.

In closing, across these areas—the resilience of the network, the performance of the business and the investments we're making for the future—the direction is clear. NBN is delivering modern, high performance, sovereign, digital infrastructure that will underpin Australia's economic and social development for decades to come. We're delivering on our commitments, strengthening the network and improving the experience for Australians who rely on it every day. Thank you, Chair, and I welcome the committee's questions.

text: The Australian published that article without any reference to Fitch. They didn't talk to Fitch about the review that was put out, and, subsequent to the article, Fitch contacted the Australian and corrected the inaccuracies in the article. What I can tell you is that Fitch, previous to this, last issued its guidance in September of 2025, the same month that we launched our Accelerate Great program and made estimates around what that program would do in their own light. They don't have access to our information. With the benefit of a year of actual data, they were able to adjust those forecasts. It wasn't so much as a reduction in their forecast. It was a correction in their forecasting. If the Australian journalist had contacted Fitch, that's what Fitch would have told them.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The picture from Fitch was not a good one, and that is because of the amount of debt being carried by NBN. Could you please update the committee on your debt levels and the impact that that is having on your credit rating? I understand your credit rating hasn't changed, but you are carrying an enormous amount of debt, and so I would just ask if you could explain both that and also the general concerns in relation to your future financial projections as to managing that debt.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: There are a couple of questions in there, so if I can just deal with them one at a time. Firstly, Fitch reinforced their rating. They didn't issue any concern. They reinforced our rating at a stable outlook. So there was no change in that rating. And in fact—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, I didn't say there was. I made that very clear.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No, but just to go to the credibility of the forward view. Secondly, we have been just recently rated by the Japanese credit rating agency as AA, which is consistent with the ratings that we see with Fitch and Moody's. We are currently sitting at 8.95 times net debt to EBITDA, and I would note that only a few years ago that was at 13 times. We have a trajectory that is seeing a reduction in that to investment grade between four and six times net debt to EBITDA. We find that the current debt levels are manageable. We just raised US$600 million in the US market in 144A market at record levels for NBN, at levels that had never been achieved before, recognising the confidence that investors have in the NBN story.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Can I just ask you what are the maturity dates and the refinancing amounts for each year to 2030, and how much of the $27.45 billion in net debt must be refinanced at materially higher interest rates compared to what has been available in recent years?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, Senator; is the question around the FY 2030 refinance?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What are the maturity dates and the refinancing amounts for each year to 2030?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Roughly, we have approximately $3 billion of debt to raise each year, and that's consistent with what we've done historically. That usually requires us to raise money through the bond markets in the European market, the US market and the Australian market. We also have existing syndicated facilities with Australian banks and a number of international banks to maintain our liquidity. As far as your question as to the cost of debt is concerned, yes, when some of this debt was raised, it was raised at record lows, when, in fact, interest rates were close to zero. But what I would say, then, is that the margin, the spread that was being paid, was quite high. As rates increase, we're seeing that margin come down. I think that's demonstrated by the 10-year bond prior to the one we've just raised, which was in FY23. We raised that one at a higher cost compared to the most recent one, by just a couple of points. That's because, while the underlying treasuries went up over that period of time, the spreads came down because of the confidence. So, in fact, we're raising, in that bond alone—it's cheaper than it was three years ago.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. I asked for the maturity dates and refinancing amounts for each year to 2030. Do you have those?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I would have to take that question on notice. In our publicly disclosed information, we have the forward curve, but we don't have each of the bonds with each of the dates specified. I would have to take that as a question on notice.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. Ms Sweeney, could you please explain your projections in relation to upgrades to higher speeds. I'm trying to understand what your forward projections are in relation to your revenues. I'm raising concerns. You've had some robust expectations as to the percentage of Australians who would move on to the higher speeds, but it looks like those expectations are not being met. Could you please talk me through that and what impact that will have on revenues.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I think it's fair to say that the Accelerate Great program, which we ran last year—close to 49.4 per cent of Australians are on 100 megabits and above as of today, and 39.9 per cent of Australians are on 500 megabits and above today. The data point to share with you is that, in September of last year, four per cent of Australians were on 500 megabits and above. And, today, as we see more customers moving to fibre and more orders coming into our business, 76 per cent or 78 per cent of those are for high-speed tiers as well. So, at the moment—I can't give you a projection out to 2030. As you know, we're restricted in terms of the projections we can give, based on the debt markets that we are in. But, today, we are tracking ahead of our high-speed tier forecast in the integrated operating plan for this year.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Can you walk me through that. What is that forecast?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: For this year?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: In terms of the 49 per cent that we expected to be on 100 megabits—we're about four basis points ahead of that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Have you got data from recent years so we can have a look at how that is tracking? Do you have anything available to you right now that you can walk me through?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Of how we're tracking over the last year?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's right, yes.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I can share with you that four per cent of Australians last year were on 500 megabits and above, and, today, 39.9 per cent are. That's a significant uplift in terms of Australians' being able to access value on our high-speed tier networks which are fibre and HFC. So, again, we are tracking ahead of where we expected to be on that. Again, I'd have to say that a lot of that goes to the great work from the retail service providers. If you've been watching the market, you will have seen that it's incredibly competitive at the moment, and we're seeing great offers for Australians around that 500-megabits-per-second price point. It's great to see Australians being able to realise that value, get better speeds and go on to fibre—a much better customer experience as well.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Can you update me on the transition to the Amazon LEOsat from Sky Muster?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sure. Gav, do you want to take that one?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'd probably characterise the program in two parts. There's the piece of the program that involves us working with retailers to build a product that we can sell, and there's the part of the program in Amazon's world, which is about launching rockets and getting rockets into space. In the first part, since we were last here, we've concluded initial product consultation with retailers and stakeholders, and that incorporated the settings for the product design for the NBN satellite product with Amazon Leo. It included transitional arrangements for existing Sky Muster customers—some operational arrangements that we'd be entering into with retailers and the like. Clearly, there's a really strong imperative that we get that transition right. That consultation was done carefully with not just retailers but key stakeholders in regional Australia, and I'm pleased that we were able to conclude that consultation recently. Right now, in terms of the product development—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, I just want to step back here. You entered into an agreement with Amazon in July 2025?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Correct.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That was announced in August 2025. The service is intending to reach more than 300,000 eligible premises to ultimately replace Sky Muster.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Correct.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: How long is it going to take for the new satellite to be available?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's not a single satellite. What we'll be utilising is—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The system of satellites.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: a constellation. There are two parts to that answer. One part is building a product that retailers can sell, and the other part is having a constellation, which Amazon has, covering the nation. If I just conclude my comments about the product development—we're in the process now of installing production terminals so we can achieve what we've already signalled to industry as a tech trial commencing this side of Christmas. We've indicated to industry that we'll be trialling and commencing commercial services in 2027. That part was and always will be a function of Amazon being able to get satellites in the air. Amazon have announced that they've now got 1,000 satellites produced—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But they're not in the sky.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's a problem, isn't it?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Amazon have launched about 400. They've publicly announced imminent launches with heavy-lift vehicles such as the—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: And Starlink has got about 10,000 or so satellites in the sky?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's right.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So how are you going to be able to compete? My understanding is that there is an up to two-year delay to book a rocket to get the satellite into space.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: NBN doesn't book rockets. Amazon—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not saying you do. Amazon is encountering massive issues trying to get their satellites in the sky. How can you possibly suggest that this is going to be ready by 2027?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What I've said is that we'll commence services at this stage. We're looking at commencing trials and commercial services in calendar year 2027, and the rollout, which we've indicated through our consultation with industry, will move progressively from the southern part of the continent to the north. If we take a step back—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, Mr Williams. The satellites aren't in the sky. They're nowhere near being ready, and you're suggesting that the rollout can start from 2027. Why would any Australian look to move onto your LEOsat service rather than Starlink, which is very advanced and already providing a brilliant service to thousands of Australians?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What Sky Muster customers and prospective customers can take comfort in is that we've consulted on a product. We are building a product that will be available progressively, from the southern part of the continent through to the northern part of the continent. We will not be launching a product—perhaps I had better explain that the way that the product would be rolled out is progressive, from the south to the north of the continent. You need satellites in space for two reasons. One is to get coverage, and one is to get depth of coverage. We plan to launch from Tasmania progressively north and we will launch at a point where we have sufficient coverage and sufficient depth of coverage to give us confidence that we can offer a great service for Australians who are in the remote parts of the country that rely on our service.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Williams, let's cut to the chase here. You cannot possibly hope to offer a great service based on the current situation with Amazon satellites, knowing the lag time in launching those satellites. Can I put to you that it is just not tenable that this service will be ready by 2027 to properly offer Australians. Ms Sweeney, can I go back to you—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We would have a different view on that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Ms Sweeney, well before you were the CEO, Mr Williams and I were talking about Sky Muster and the deficiencies with Sky Muster and the advantages that Starlink presented. Starlink is now a very sophisticated service that many thousands of Australians are using.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They're a global platform, and, as you know, through UOMO, they are an integrated full stack. So they're a formidable competitor.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: So why didn't the Australian government contract with Starlink rather than Amazon? Amazon's got 400 satellites in the air and can't do the job for a continent the size of Australia. Starlink has 10,000 satellites and is able to offer full coverage right now.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: As you're aware, we did go through thorough due diligence and RFP around that. Without going into the details, Amazon was chosen for very good reasons.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What were those reasons, given it cannot provide the service at the moment?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's not correct. We will be in test in December of this year; we will be in Tasmania in test. We have already been able to, again, provide the antennas and actually test the solution already and test on our production systems as well. So, again, we have every confidence with Amazon. They will release first. I'm not sure if you know this. In the US, Canada, Germany, France, the UK and Argentina, they'll go live first, and then Australia will go to the commercial launch. Amazon are incredibly committed to this, as you can imagine. They are also a global integrated player. They've also made decisions around UOMO in the US around some of the access into other businesses as well. They're heavily committed in terms of the Australian footprint. Just to be clear, we don't need 10,000 satellites to work in Australia.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's 3,200. That is the constellation size for the Amazon constellation. The initial rollout—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Through Starlink.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. Amazon have announced that the initial constellation that they are building to is 3,200-odd satellites. I don't have the numbers of their announcement—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When will they get 3,200 satellites into the sky?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I don't have the announcements that they've made around the number of launches that they've got committed. But you're right to say that the program requires a significant launch manifest by Amazon. There are a few launches. Underneath that imperative includes getting some heavy-lift launch vehicles in the sky, such as the Arianespace Ariane 64, which is scheduled for a launch in November, and the ULA Vulcan Centaur. What you'll see with these heavy-lift vehicles is the Arianespace vehicle can carry 36 satellites at each launch and the Vulcan Centaur would have about 45 satellites. So the 14 missions that Amazon have currently undertaken—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Sorry, I'm starting to giggle. I appreciate that Amazon has great aspirations to fill the sky full of satellites, but the fact is they're not in the sky. Australians are looking to NBN as an alternative to Sky Muster, but why would any Australian sign up to the NBN for satellite services when, Ms Sweeney, the best you can do currently is offer a testing capability in Tasmania by the end of the year? So when will you be able to cover the continent with LEO-sat services which are equivalent to Starlink? When will that happen?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Again, we've been consistent with the commentary that we would be in test in December of 2026 and we would go live in 2027.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: In Tasmania, just—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Outside of that, I really can't give you dates. As you rightly point out, we are reliant—

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's very important that we have some understanding of what the projections are. What has Amazon told you about when you will be able to ensure that, if an Australian signs up, no matter where they live in this large continent, they will be able to access the satellite service offered by NBN? When will that date be?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I can't give you the date. It's reliant, as Mr Williams has already mentioned, on the launch schedules. We are working through it with Amazon. We don't control the schedules of Amazon's global rocket launches or the constellations, but what we are doing is working very closely with them. We have Amazon in Australia this week working with our team and, again, looking to make sure that, when we do go live—and I think this is incredibly important as the statutory infrastructure provider—customers who are on the geostationary solution have a great transition to that LEO solution.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But what are they transitioning onto and when will that happen?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They're transitioning onto the product that we have consulted with industry on and are building. That's—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But you can't tell us when that will be made available to all Australians?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When it'll be made available will be a function of Amazon getting sufficient satellites. It is a big job to be done in launching those rockets—there is no question, Senator.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I don't disagree with you at all. I'm just raising concerns.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: And I think it's a great thing that there's competition in regional and remote communications, where, over decades, there hasn't been. A decade ago we used to talk about the data drought. People don't talk about the data drought anymore. What we're about here is, across regional communications, pushing fibre deeper, as Ms Sweeney said in her opening comments, such that now, of the circa 3.7 million homes and businesses in regional Australia, about 2.7 million of those will be upgradeable to fibre—in fact, 90 per cent of those now. We've got an upgraded fixed wireless network, which includes speeds getting up to 500 megabits per second on our over-provisioned 400 megabit per second plan. Here, for the—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: As a result of a lot of work and investment by the former coalition government.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I use the service almost every day. It's a marvellous service. The job to be done for the last 300 is to embrace the technology that wasn't available when we launched Sky Muster services.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Of course. I realise that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Now we are working with a pioneering partner such as Amazon to utilise their global constellation. We will not launch until we have the product that we've defined with industry operating with a great grade of service for our customers. Frankly, on the timing imperative, we have fuel in our Sky Muster satellites beyond the time that we think that we'll—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: But you just need the rockets. You need the rocket to get the satellite into the sky.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: For our replacement product, we do, yes.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's right.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We'll be watching with interest Kourou in French Guiana in November as the Arianespace 64 launches with the next 36 satellites. That will start getting the balance of the thousand or so that have already been produced to the constellation of 3,200 or so, which will be the full complement of—
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Do you know how long it will take to get the 3,200 satellites into the air?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That's Amazon's role, and I'm sure that they'll be making announcements.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You must have been given some sort of forecast.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We work with Amazon consistently, and we take our own views as to timing.
witness_position: Chief Development Officer, Regional and Remote

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I would like all correspondence between you and Amazon in relation to this service since 1 July last year, please. We need to understand what's going on.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We'll take it on notice.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: If this is being held out to Australians as an alternative service to Starlink, we need to understand what the projections are. I find it difficult to comprehend that, when you've entered into such a massive contract, you can't provide more detail. What is the value of that contract, by the way?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'd have to come back to you on that.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You don't have a ballpark figure for me?

text: Welcome, Mr Paul Graham, the group chief executive and managing director. I welcome your team and, I'm sure, others assisting either from the back of the room or offsite. Do you wish to make an opening statement, Mr Graham?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
I do, Chair, thank you. Before I begin, I'd just like to acknowledge Dr Helen Haines and the horrific attack she suffered last week. I've dealt with Dr Haines in this house, and she's always been a great supporter of Australia Post. Our thoughts are obviously with her, her family, her team and the local Indi community, and we wish her strength and courage in her recovery.

I'd like to start by acknowledging the traditional custodians, the Ngunnawal and Ngambri peoples, and pay my respects to their elders.

There has been an increased amount of press and parliamentary coverage in relation to our post office network in recent months. I want to take this opportunity and place on the public record our absolute commitment to maintaining 4,000 postal outlets across Australia, with 2,500 of those in regional, rural and remote Australia. It is not only enshrined in our regulatory framework; it forms a core part of our overall strategy at Australia Post.

Regional Australia remains at the centre of our investment for a stronger Australia Post. We're now supporting communities where a traditional post office has never been practical. In partnership with Outback Stores, we've opened 16 new community postal agencies in remote communities, many of them in Indigenous owned stores. Eleven are in the Northern Territory, with others in Western Australia and Queensland. These communities can now send and receive mail and parcels close to home without long journeys.

Our focus on regional Australia is not only on maintaining our post office footprint but also on ensuring that reliable and cost-effective parcel delivery can be maintained. That is why we continue to invest in new parcel facilities in places like Morwell, building on the 10 new facilities we announced this past year, all in regional towns, all to help grow local businesses. Ecommerce growth in the regions is outstripping the growth of metro, demonstrating that our investments are making it easier and more convenient for people to access products in these regional, rural and remote areas.

Our commitment to communities goes beyond our network. During Mental Health Month, we announced more than $700,000 in community grants for 81 community led projects that build connection and support mental health and wellbeing. More than half of these grants are going to rural and remote areas.

At the same time, the way Australians live, work and shop is rapidly changing, and customers are looking for longer hours of access and more convenience. We've responded by broadening how and where people can use our services, including through parcel lockers and other self-service options. Importantly, these are in addition to our reported retail outlets. They're designed to complement our post offices, not replace them.

Our licenced post offices remain vital to their communities, and, as more Australians shop online, parcels now make up the majority of their transactions. Commissions to licensees have increased every year for the past 17 years and reached a record $635 million last financial year. Additionally, our renegotiated Bank@Post agreements, which now include ANZ, have lifted those commissions by 30 per cent.

Let me be clear: we are not seeking to reduce LPO services. Where third parties and government agencies have moved online and ended arrangements with Australia Post, we're seeking new ones, with an expression of interest process underway for additional over-the-counter services. Where licensees choose to retire or leave the network, our priority is continuity of service for those communities. For two years we've been working with licensees and their associations to modernise an LPO model that's more than 30 years old, and that work continues.

However, the challenges for LPOs in metropolitan and non-metropolitan areas are not like for like. For LPOs in regional, rural and remote Australia, we propose to provide an additional $30 million in commissions each year, with targeted support for those outlets that need it most. The challenges in metropolitan areas are largely due to significant geographical overlap. We remain committed to exploring opportunities to strengthen and improve their financial sustainability.

Importantly, Australia Post maintains its nationwide network without the support of taxpayer funding. We remain one of the only major postal operators in the world that delivers on our government mandated service obligations on a fully self-funded basis.

Australia Post is about to enter the busiest time of the year. Australians are increasingly reliant on ecommerce to find the lowest possible price to help in the current cost-of-living crisis. At the end of next month, Black Friday will mark the start of what we expect to be our biggest peak delivery on record. Last year, we delivered almost 111 million parcels across November and December, including more than three million on a single day for the first time. This year, we are preparing to deliver more than 120 million parcels.

To meet this anticipated demand, we've recruited 3,900 casual team members and expanded our air network. Last month, together with Qantas, we welcomed the first three additional airbus A321 freighters based at the new 24-hour freight terminal at Western Sydney International Airport.

None of this work or the services we provide are possible without our people. Our team members, licensees and delivery partners will once again work long hours over the coming weeks so that Australians receive the gifts, medicines and essentials they rely on. I want to sincerely thank them for their continued dedication. They are the beating heart of the community that we serve.

Finally, last week I announced my intention to retire in June next year. I remain fully committed to supporting customers and our team members right up until the last minute of my last day, working hard to keep our people safe, delight our customers and communities, and ensure our long-term sustainability. I'm happy to take questions.

witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. If you look at the footnote on page 183, you'll see the reference to the $48.9 million profit. That's in the footnotes, Mr Graham.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That would be right in terms of the calculation.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Reserved letters—$48.9 million profit. The cost of living for so many Australians is a massive issue. portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'd better take that on notice, Senator. Just for value, the average household consumes about six to eight stamps a year, and therefore the last cost increase—whilst any cost increase is, obviously, going to hurt—was about a dollar to the average household per annum.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I want to quickly turn to the Gaius e-bikes. Thank you for providing that further information. That cost $18.2 million. You indicated you were going to be able to provide the injury data in the information that you hold. Have you got that further information that you can hand up to us?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have a broad range of safety data. We don't have data recorded at an individual-piece-of-equipment level. What I can say on the Gaius is that we had no significant injuries reported. What we had reported was fatigue, predominantly, in relation to those vehicles. We introduced those vehicles into the fleet predominantly to reduce the motorbike rounds that we have and which are the most dangerous rounds of all. We did full testing of those vehicles along with the union and with relative experts, and that testing provided very positive feedback. However, nothing replaces testing in reality. As we put those bikes into service and we looked at the different terrains that they were on, we were getting feedback from our team members about fatigue and about certain terrains on which they maybe didn't operate to the optimum level. As a precaution, we pulled that fleet off—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Mr Graham, this is a pretty serious issue—$18.2 million spent on acquiring 500 e-trikes from Taiwan which were not fit for purpose.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They were fit for purpose in relation to the testing that we had done and in the trials that we conducted with specialists—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They were not fit for purpose in relation to the purpose for which you acquired them.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I dispute that.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm not going to live on an alternative planet to yours, Mr Graham. You withdrew the vehicles.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: As a precaution based on—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Right!

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: feedback from our team members.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Right!

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Of course, safety is the most important thing, because we were getting feedback that, on certain terrains—not all team members were complaining about the bikes. But, as a precaution, we withdrew all bikes from the fleet—as we would do, in common sense—to ensure that we validated any of the feedback that we got, just in case it was more widely spread than we anticipated. We didn't have a significant number of complaints, but, again, as a precaution, we withdrew those bikes from the fleet. We have now taken some of that feedback; we have worked with independent experts. We have applied different changes to that bike and have now started to redeploy them back into action.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You've indicated you're going to redeploy a hundred or so.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: One hundred and fifty—we're starting with the redeployment of 150, and we'll continue to take feedback. This is no different to the other EVs that we have in our fleet. We're now on the fifth version of those bikes. We continue to take feedback from our team members and continue to look at how to improve both the rideability of those vehicles as well as the safety.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay. What changes have you made to the e-trikes? They'll be used for a different purpose, for delivering to—parcel delivery?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: They will, and they will also go back to being used for the original task that they were intended for—but, again, with modifications. As I say, every piece of equipment we've introduced in relation to ride-on vehicles—we've always made modifications after a series of field testing. There's a list—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Why didn't you conduct the testing beforehand?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We did.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You spent $18.2 million. You went out and bought 500 e-trikes. Can I put to you that you didn't do the appropriate testing. You should have done the testing prior to the acquisition, because that's an enormous amount of money to lose.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Secondly—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: No. Let's be clear here. There's an $18.2 million acquisition. They were all taken off the road and put in warehouses. You're going to redeploy 150 only. Is that correct?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We're starting to redeploy. In the first batch of redeployment are about 150 vehicles.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: And what's going to happen to the rest of them?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, that wasn't clear, to be frank, in your answer to the question on notice. So you're going to be redeploying all of the vehicles?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That would be our intention. Again, we're taking caution to deploy the 150 with the modifications to make sure those modifications are indeed going to ensure that those vehicles are the safest possible. We did extensive testing before we purchased those vehicles, in line with external experts as well as with the union involved heavily with that testing. However, nothing replaces real-life, on-the-road, day-to-day work. And, as we deployed those vehicles—and, obviously, in a testing environment, it's impossible to deploy those vehicles in every single part of Australia. We found, as we deployed them into different types of terrain and as they were up against different road conditions, that we were getting feedback that they were causing issues with the team members, fatigue being predominantly one of them, in relation to how the bike actually rides. As a precaution, we—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Why were people getting fatigued?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It's because of the nature of the way that the bike actually moves and also because of the way that the bike has to sit as they are putting mail into a letterbox. It's the turning movement. Also, because the bike sits on a gyro, they found on certain terrains, not all terrains, that it was more fatiguing in their arms and shoulders.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thanks very much, Mr Graham.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Thank you for appearing again tonight. There have been six inquiries into various aspects of Australia Post in the last six years, and yet the future of rural and regional Australia Post outlets is no more clear, let alone secure. Liberal-National and Labor-Greens governments—it makes no difference. The agenda keeps rolling. Now we have inquiry No. 7 coming up, which I'll ask you about in a minute. Across the last six years, the number of post offices has reduced by 208. So, Mr Graham, how many post offices are due to close in the next 12 months and in the next six months, before you leave?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Currently, as I sit here, we have three post offices that we've announced the closure of. We don't have any other post offices that I'm aware of in relation to being closed. As I've said before at estimates, we do not control the licensee network and, unfortunately, we do see from time to time licensees providing virtually no notice and closing up shop due to various conditions—illness, dispute with the landlord et cetera. But, as I sit here today, we have three post offices that we've already announced that will be closing and we do not have any other post offices in the next six months that I'm aware of, putting aside those that could be decided by the licensee themselves.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Have you ever reopened a post office after closing it?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have reopened a number of post offices that have been closed, and we opened, I think, 14 new post offices last year. Each one is judged on its merits and in relation to the needs and services that that community requires. As I said in my opening statement, our goal is to preserve the 4,000 post offices that we are regulated to provide, particularly the 2½ thousand in regional, rural and remote areas. We are committed to doing that, indeed, by providing an extra $30 million in commissions for those LPOs in those regional, rural and remote areas, because they are seeing a decline in foot traffic and a decline in traditional usage that customers have for post offices.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Could you give me on notice, please, the number of post offices that have closed, including 2000 to 2026?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes. I believe that we have issued a similar response before to a QON. We will certainly provide that to you.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It is also the number of post offices reopened and the number of new post offices that were never in operation before—2020 to 2026.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Yes, we can provide that information.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: How many new post offices serving new residential areas, not rebuilds, opened in the last 12 months, and how many more are planned?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I defer to Mr Bannister, who runs that network. I can say that, for example, Oran Park in Western Sydney is a new one that we've opened—a large growing area of young families. Again, working with the local member of parliament and the local community, we saw the need to put in a full-service post office. We've opened that post office, but I'll defer to my colleague Mr Bannister.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Last financial year, there were 72 post offices that closed and there were 54 that opened. That was a net reduction of 18. Often a post office will close for unplanned reasons. There are many reasons why a post office may close, including a licensee choosing not to continue, and that may result in a short period whereby the post office is not able to operate where it previously was. Our team worked tirelessly to replace those post offices, particularly in rural, regional and remote Australia, where we know that they add value. At the same time, in metropolitan Australia we are expanding with growth corridors. You think of the north- and south-west growth corridors of Sydney. There are obviously huge growth corridors in the likes of Melbourne and Brisbane, and we're actively bringing new postal services. But I will take that question on notice as to the number, but the number would be well beyond 20.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Coleambally is a good example, Senator, where the licensee closed at short notice. We were able to put in a very quick temporary solution with the local pharmacy in relation to providing mail and basic parcel services. That has now expanded to become a full licensed post office environment, and that means that that town can continue to enjoy those full postal services. But it does relate to the unique circumstances of that particular area.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: When an LPO decide they can't remain in business and, as a result, give the 90-day notice to hand back their licence, Australia Post is required, as I understand it, to advertise an urgent expression of interest to find a new licensee. How many advices have you received of a desire to hand back, and, of those, how many were subject to an expression of interest and how many resulted in the post office remaining open? Give me whatever period you have. The last 12 months are of special interest.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'll take that on notice, but again—and I'll defer to my colleague Mr Bannister—we always run an expression of interest and have a detailed consultation program for the community.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We'll take the question on notice to ensure that we give you the most accurate information for the last financial year. I'd again refer to the 72 that closed and the work that was done by the team to replace as many of those as we could, particularly in regional, rural and remote Australia.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The service mandate for 4,000 post offices does not specify which type of outlet, but two-thirds of licensees are looking to retire over the next three years. Is it your intention to maintain this guarantee by converting full service LPOs to community post offices, offering a small subset of post office services and still calling them post offices? For clarity, the reason is profit.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text:
Again, our goal is to ensure that the community receive the services that they require. We do not make any more money by closing a licensee or having a licensee closed. Our goal is to meet our commitment to maintaining 4,000 post offices, including the 2½ thousand in rural, regional and remote Australia. What we do is look at the circumstances of that community and what services they are making available to them, and we try and make sure that we are replicating the services that community wants. Each case is quite unique. In metropolitan, built-up areas, we're finding that a lot of the consumers don't want a full-service post office; what they want is 24/7 access to parcels, and therefore they want more parcel focused formats or parcel lockers. But we do agree that in regional Australia it still is very much the traditional post office. But we do have, for example, towns like Shepparton, which has 21 post offices, so there are a significant number in certain regional towns. Our goal, when a post office closes, is to look at that town, look at the needs that that town has and ensure that we can replicate the services they require both today and going forward.

As I've said many times in front of estimates committees, this is becoming an ongoing challenge for licensees. I think, as you say, this has been communicated over many years, but we will be seeing the apex of that in the coming years due to the ongoing decline in foot traffic for traditional services because of digitisation as well as the ageing demographic of a lot of these licensees, particularly in regional Australia.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The reimagined concept turns post offices into a retail amusement park, relying on significant foot traffic, limiting the potential outlets and doing nothing to solve the problems of rural and remote community post offices. How will you add profitability, meaning long-term viability, to rural and remote post offices? I know you said that it's difficult.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It is difficult. We have some post offices in regional areas that flourish and do very well. We have others that are really struggling. That's why—
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Have you done any research into what makes a category flourish versus stagnate?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: We have data. A lot of it is basically about the changing nature of how people want to interface with the post office.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: That varies from town to town?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: It does. Where we have an older demographic, we find that more over-the-counter services and traditional services are favoured, where with a younger demographic it is digital. They want a digital interaction. We have put, as part of LPO Reimagined, an investment of $30 million and additional commissions into regional, rural and remote Australia to sustain those post offices, in particular those that we know are marginal, to ensure that those services are maintained. As I said in my opening statement, it's a different scenario in metropolitan areas, where we've got significant overlap which has been built up over many, many years, In regional, rural and remote areas, it is about sustaining the existing services, paying more commissions to those post offices that are on the margin and making sure that those services, particularly where we are the only bank in town or the only provider of Billpay—we know they're essential services to those communities, and they must be maintained.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Are you okay, Minister?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I was just nodding because I live in a regional town, and the Trinity Beach LPO is a fantastic post office.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: The next question is to you. Christine Holgate at Team Global Express has a proposal to use rural and regional Australia Post outlets to provide last-leg delivery services alongside Australia Post's own service. This will provide significant revenue for underutilised LPOs and provide options for the public. What is Australia Post's position on this proposal?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: You'll have to ask Australia Post.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I'm happy to answer that and I believe I've answered this question many times in Senate estimates. TGE are a private equity owned business. They have the ability to invest in their own network. Indeed, on their website they claim they have one of the largest networks in the country. We already provide open access to our network. Last year we moved 90 million parcels on behalf of our competitors. We pay more than double the market rate to our licensees for the provision of service for those parcels. There is a low barrier to entry in relation to parcels. What our competitors want to do is basically lower their own costs of operation, and what they will then do is try to take our market share, particularly in the metropolitan areas, which are the high-volume markets. So we do not believe that opening up our network in the way that Ms Holgate has required is a smart or logical thing to do. It's not done anywhere else in the world because it's not a smart thing to do. We currently, as I say, have an open network where we already handle 90 million parcels on behalf of our competition.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Ms Holgate was a pretty clever operator. Is she just in this for her company?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Her company is a private equity company that has only one goal, and that is to ensure it makes money. We do not believe that that would be to the interests of Australia Post or the licensees or communities. As I said in my opening statement, the growth in non-metropolitan areas is actually significantly above the growth we see in metropolitan areas, which shows that the cost of getting parcels and the service that we are providing is allowing those regional towns to gain access to an efficient parcel service. But also, more importantly, it's allowing the small businesses in those towns who want to sell their e-commerce products into the metropolitan cities to get those parcels delivered into those metropolitan cities.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Would it be worse for you if her company started offering contracts to LPOs?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Well, they would not be allowed to do that under the current arrangements that we have with those LPOs. As I say, Ms Holgate's website says they're the largest network in Australia, so I don't see why she would need to use Australia Post.
witness_position: Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Senator Roberts, I'd like to share the call.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: I've just got one topic to go—four or five questions.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: Okay.

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
text: What was the operating profit or loss on the letters business in 2025-26?

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO

portfolio: INFRASTRUCTURE, TRANSPORT, REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT, COMMUNICATIONS, SPORT AND THE ARTS PORTFOLIO
